coredata.dc:description:
Background Since its formal recognition, Gaming Disorder (GD) has attracted significant research attention, with gaming motivation consistently identified as a key factor in its development. Among various motives for gaming, escapism shows one of the strongest and most consistent associations with problematic gaming. However, previous studies have mostly conceptualized escapism as withdrawal from the external world, overlooking the role of self-related processes.
Objectives This study aimed to distinguish between escapism from the world (EW) and escapism from the self (ES) and to examine their respective relationships with GD, stress, and well-being.
Methods A cross-sectional questionnaire-based study was conducted among 142 participants (82 women, 57 men, 3 other; M_age = 18.99, SD = .37). Validated instruments assessed gaming motives, GD symptoms, stress, well-being, and vitality. Data were analyzed using hierarchical regression and mediation models.
Results ES, but not EW, uniquely predicted GD symptoms. ES fully mediated the relationship between EW and GD, indicating that withdrawal from the external world contributes to problematic gaming only when it reflects avoidance of the Self. Similarly, ES mediated the association between stress and GD, whereas EW did not. Furthermore, ES was negatively associated with well-being and vitality, while EW showed no significant correlations.
Conclusions These findings suggest that escapism from the Self constitutes a maladaptive pathway to GD and is consistently linked with reduced well-being and vitality. In contrast, escapism from the external world alone does not appear to contribute directly to problematic gaming. Targeting self-related escapism may improve intervention strategies for GD.

ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: Since its formal recognition, Gaming Disorder (GD) has attracted significant research attention, with gaming motivation consistently identified as a key factor in its development. ce:section.ce:para: Since the introduction of Gaming Disorder (GD) as a condition warranting further study (APA, 2013), and its subsequent recognition as a behavioral addiction (WHO, 2019), research on its etiology has grown substantially. Not surprisingly, GD is understood as the result of a complex interplay between individual, game-related, and environmental factors. Among the individual factors, gaming motivation has been identified as particularly important (Király et al., 2023).

The range of reasons why people play video games is extensive. For instance, Király and colleagues (2022) identified 26 distinct motives in the Gaming Motivation Inventory. Among them, escapism has consistently been shown to exhibit a strong association with problematic gaming, as confirmed by meta-analytic evidence (Bäcklund et al., 2022; Wang & Cheng, 2022). Notably, the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (5th ed.; APA, 2013) includes the use of games as a means of escape among the nine diagnostic criteria for GD. The centrality of this motive is further reflected in psychometric operationalizations of GD, such as the Internet Gaming Disorder Scale developed by Pontes and colleagues, which explicitly incorporate items referring to escape (Pontes & Griffiths, 2015).

Although escapist play has often been linked to negative outcomes, for example, functioning as a mediator between psychological distress and gaming disorder (Maroney et al., 2018), it may also serve a protective role when it leads to positive psychological outcomes (e.g., recovery and mood management) and is followed by a smooth return to reality (Kosa & Uysal, 2020; Strojny & Strojny, 2025). We argue that this theoretical and empirical inconsistency may stem from the very definition of escapism employed in psychological research on gaming.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Escapism as a retreat from the world – limitations of bottom-up conceptualization
ce:section.ce:para: In one of the earliest conceptualizations of escapism in the context of gaming, Yee (2006) defined it as “using the online environment to avoid thinking about real life problems” (p. 774). This conceptualization emerged from earlier player-type approaches to online gameplay, particularly Bartle's (1996) taxonomy, which was developed from players' self-reports and highlighted different motivational orientations toward virtual environments.

Similarly, Demetrovics et al. (2011) defined escapism as a flight from reality, particularly from real-world problems. In constructing their motives for online gaming questionnaire, the authors relied on previously developed scales as well as qualitative insights from players. The conceptualization found in Király et al. (2022) follows this approach and is grounded in Demetrovics's work. The questionnaires developed by Demetrovics, Yee, and Király remain the most widely used instruments in the study of gaming-related escapism (Marques et al., 2023).

A focus on distancing oneself from the physical world can also be found in one of the most recent conceptualizations proposed by Giardina and colleagues (2024). In their view, escape occurs when gaming is used to avoid physical environment that undermines a person's sense of agency and stability of self-image, while escapism reflects the use of the simulated game environment as a way to compensate for difficulties experienced in real life. Both perspectives emphasize withdrawal from an external reality perceived as threatening or unwelcoming. Yet this dualistic framing, contrasting the game world with the external world seems to neglect another environment that is fundamental from a psychological standpoint: the inner world of the self.

This raises the question of whether the very concept and definition of escapism in these studies are epiphenomenal, stemming from the lack of a clear conceptual framework and the limited self-awareness of participants in qualitative research. Perhaps respondents did not so much wish to escape from reality itself, but rather from self-awareness arising from the interaction between the self and the surrounding world, an experience they were unable to articulate.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Escape to avoid the self: earlier top-down conceptualizations
ce:section.ce:para: Early conceptualizations of escapism understood it as “the pursuit of excluding unwanted beliefs from the field of consciousness” (Longeway, 1990), primarily to avoid painful self-awareness and negative emotions (Baumeister & Scher, 1988).

Both Longeway and Baumeister emphasized that escapism may, under certain circumstances, be desirable and even protective, as it can prevent individuals from falling into despair. Longeway (1990) noted: “We all employ escapism some of the time, and it is no doubt good that we do so. We don't normally call people escapists, however, unless they are habitually escapist about most beliefs they find aversive, whether they need to attend to them or not.” (p. 2). It is consistent with Lazarus and Folkman's (1984) remark that coping strategies cannot be judged as adaptive or maladaptive without considering the individual and situational context.

Researchers have devoted considerable effort to understanding the roots of self-related escapism and its correlates, as one of its most severe consequences may be suicide (Baumeister, 1990). Its origins are often linked to self-discrepancy, particularly the failure to meet important personal standards, as well as to pronounced emotional distress, difficulties in regulating negative affect, low self-concept clarity, and heightened self-awareness (Selby et al., 2008; Selimbegović et al., 2020; Zeigler-Hill et al., 2024).

Situations in which individuals develop a strong and persistent desire to avoid the self and internal experiences are typically associated with negative consequences. Hayes conceptualizes experiential avoidance as a central dimension in the etiology of a broad range of psychological disorders (Hayes et al., 1996). A heightened tendency to escape from the self has been linked to masochism and aversive self-evaluations (Zeigler-Hill et al., 2024). Avoidance motivation has also been associated with performance decrements, resource depletion, and reduced well-being (Roskes et al., 2014). Moreover, persistent self-avoidance may strengthen beliefs of threat or fear, thereby contributing to the development of anxiety disorders (Urcelay, 2024).

From this perspective, the notion that escapism may be beneficial might appear surprising. How, then, could Kosa and Uysal (2020, pp. 63–76) conclude that escapism into games may serve important psychological functions? The answer lies in how escapism is interpreted and defined in research on GD - as a withdrawal from the world. A temporary distraction from external situations that cannot be actively managed at a given moment may be beneficial (Lazarus & Folkman, 1984). For example, distracting oneself from despair and stress while waiting for medical test results may indeed facilitate stress regulation and mood management. Similarly, detachment from external expectations following a demanding effort (e.g., after passing an important exam) may function as a recovery mechanism protecting against exhaustion. In contrast, constant detachment from the self, rooted in the rejection of one's self-image and a lack of acceptance of who one is, seems far less likely to produce positive outcomes (Hayes et al., 1996). Consistent with this view, Kwon et al. (2009) demonstrated a positive association between self-discrepancy, negative mood, self-escapism, and gaming disorder.

ce:section.ce:section-title: The core of escapism in gaming disorder: escaping the self or escaping the world?
ce:section.ce:para: As stated earlier, it is important to distinguish between escapism from the world (EW) and escapism from the self (ES). While temporary distraction from real-life problems may function as a coping strategy (Melodia et al., 2020), the persistent desire to run away from oneself is more problematic. This distinction may help clarify the potential positive effects of escapism.

First, based on Baumeister and Scher (1988) conceptualization of escapism, we assume that ES will better predict GD than EW (Hypothesis 1). Moreover, the main mechanism underlying the observed association between EW and GD is how the individual perceives the self. If EW contributes to negative self-evaluation and avoidance of the self, only then will it lead to problematic gaming. Put more briefly, ES mediates the relationship between EW and GD (Hypothesis 2).

According to Maroney et al. (2018), life stress is associated with GD through the escape motive. Their research shows that only when life stress prompts individuals to seek escape as a coping strategy may it contribute to problematic gaming. In light of Longeway (1990) work, however, the problem does not lie in using escapism as a temporary detachment from problems, which can be either harmful or beneficial depending on the context (Lazarus & Folkman, 1984). The problem arises when avoidance of the self becomes a habitual pattern. Thus, our third hypothesis is that ES, but not EW, mediates the relationship between stress and GD (Hypothesis 3).

Finally, considering prior work highlighting the potential positive outcomes of escapism, we argue that such effects may occur when gaming serves as a distraction from real-life problems. In contrast, when escapism reflects the desire to avoid the self, it is detrimental. Therefore, ES, but not EW, is expected to be a negative predictor of well-being and vitality (Hypothesis 4).

The study sample included 142 participants (82 women, 57 men, 3 other; M = 18.99, SD = .37), all first-year students of [blinded for review]. Their mean weekly gaming time was 8.28 h (SD = 7.17). They represented 16 different faculties, with the vast majority coming from fields other than psychology. Recruitment was conducted through official university emails distributed by faculty dean's offices to all first-year students studying on campus. Students who were interested in participation responded to the invitation, attended an in-person meeting during which informed consent was obtained, and completed the study online. Participants received a monetary reward for participation (40 PLN; approximately €10). The present study was based on the first wave of a longitudinal project, which is why recruitment was limited to a single student cohort and participant compensation had to remain within the available project budget.
Eligibility required a minimum of 1 h of gameplay per week. An attention check item was included, and participants who failed it were automatically excluded.
The dataset referenced in this study is available upon request.

Ethics and informed consent. The study involved anonymous, voluntary participation and posed no more than minimal risk to participants. According to institutional policies applicable at the affiliating institution, this type of anonymous, minimal-risk questionnaire study did not require prior review and approval by an Institutional ethics committee. All participants received study information and provided informed consent prior to participation. Participants could discontinue at any time without penalty. Data were analyzed in anonymized form.

Escapism from world and from Self. The dimension of escapism from the world was assessed with relevant items from the Gaming Motivation Inventory (Király et al., 2022), Polish translation. The result was calculated as a sum of values of 4 items comprising factor Escape. Cronbach's alpha was .92 in the present sample.

The escapism from Self dimension was measured with items created for the purpose of this study. These items were developed as conceptually corresponding adaptations of the world-focused escapism items derived from the Gaming Motivation Inventory (Király et al., 2022). The rationale was to preserve a broadly comparable item structure while shifting the target of escapist motivation from external reality and everyday problems to self-focused awareness, self-evaluation, and identity-related experience. Thus, rather than generating a broad initial item pool, we constructed four self-focused items intended to parallel the established world-focused scale at the level of general motivational logic.

The Subjective Vitality Scale (Ryan & Frederick, 1997), in its Polish adaptation by Mudło-Głagolska (2020), was used. The scale comprises 7 items rated on a 5-point Likert scale (1 = Not at all true, 5 = Very true). In the present study, internal consistency was satisfactory (Cronbach's α = .88).

The Internet Gaming Disorder Scale – Short Form (IGDS9-SF; Pontes & Griffiths, 2015) was used in its Polish adaptation by Schivinski et al. (2018). The scale consists of nine items assessing gaming-related behaviors over the past 12 months. Responses were given on a 5-point Likert scale (1 = Never, 5 = Very often). Internal consistency in the present study was high (Cronbach's α = .75).

Well-Being was measured with the Satisfaction With Life Scale (SWLS; Diener et al., 1985), using the Polish adaptation by Juczyński (2001). The scale consists of five items. Internal consistency in the present sample was satisfactory (Cronbach's α = .81).

Stress was measured with the 10-item Perceived Stress Scale (PSS-10; Cohen et al., 1983), adapted into Polish (Ogińska-Bulik & Juczyński, 2009). The questionnaire consists of 10 items rated on a 5-point Likert scale (0 = never to 4 = very often), referring to experiences during the last month. Four positively worded items (items 4, 5, 7, and 8) are reverse-scored. The total score is obtained by summing all items and ranges from 0 to 40, with higher scores indicating greater perceived stress. In the present study, the internal consistency of the scale was high (α = .89).

Because the analyses were not pre-registered, the results should be interpreted with caution and regarded as exploratory. Hypothesis 1
ES as a stronger predictor of GD than EW
Both escapism from the world and escapism from the self, when analyzed separately, were correlated with GD (see Table 2).

To assess their relative contribution, we conducted two hierarchical regression analyses. In the first model EW was entered in Step 1, followed by ES in Step 2. The increase in explained variance was statistically significant, indicating that adding ES improved the model. In contrast, in the second model, when ES was entered first and EW was added in the second step, the increase in explained variance was not significant. The results of these hierarchical regressions are presented in Table 3 . Hypothesis 2
ES fully mediates relation between EW and GD

A mediation analysis was conducted using PROCESS Model 4 (Hayes, 2022), with EW as the predictor, ES as the mediator, and GD as the outcome (N = 142). All variables were standardized prior to the analysis.
EW significantly predicted ES, β = .65, SE = .07, t(138) = 9.89, p < .001, 95% CI [.52, .78].

The overall model predicting GD was significant, R
2 = .26, F(2, 139) = 24.09, p < .001. As shown in Fig. 1 , escapism from world predicted gaming disorder indirectly through escapism from self. In this model, ES was a significant positive predictor of GD, β = .39, SE = .09, t(138) = 4.29, p < .001, 95% CI [.21, .57], whereas the direct effect of EW on GD was not significant, β = .13, SE = .09, t(138) = 1.43, p = .15, 95% CI [–.05, .31].

The indirect effect of EW on GD through ES was significant, effect = .25, 95% bootstrap CI [.11, .42]. This pattern indicates full mediation, such that the relationship between escapism from world and gaming disorder was entirely accounted for by escapism from the Self. Hypothesis 3
Mediating role of ES but not EW in the relationship between stress and GD

In the first step, we examined the relationship between stress and GD. Stress emerged as a significant positive predictor of GD, β = .30, SE = .08, t(140) = 3.76, p < .001, 95% CI [.14, .46]. The model accounted for a significant proportion of variance in GD, R2 = .09, F(1, 140) = 14.12, p < .001.

A parallel mediation analysis was conducted using PROCESS Model 4 (Hayes, 2022), with stress as the predictor, ES and EW as parallel mediators, and GD as the outcome (N = 142). The parallel mediation model is presented in Fig. 2 . All variables were standardized prior to the analysis.

When the mediators were introduced into the model, stress positively predicted both of them: EW, β = .36, SE = .08, t(140) = 4.58, p < .001, 95% CI [.21, .52], and ES, β = .45, SE = .08, t(140) = 5.92, p < .001, 95% CI [.30, .60].

The overall model with two mediators was significant, R2 = .26, F(3, 138) = 16.47, p < .001. In this model, ES was a significant positive predictor of GD, β = .38, SE = .10, t(138) = 3.77, p < .001, 95% CI [.18, .57], whereas the direct effect of stress, β = .09, SE = .08, t(138) = 1.08, p = .28, 95% CI [−.07, .25], and the effect of EW, β = .13, SE = .10, t(138) = 1.31, p = .19, 95% CI [−.06, .31], were not significant.

The total indirect effect of stress on GD was significant, effect = .21, 95% bootstrap CI [.11, .33]. The specific indirect effect through ES was significant, effect = .17, 95% bootstrap CI [.06, .30], whereas the indirect effect through EW was not, effect = .05, 95% bootstrap CI [−.02, .12]. This pattern suggests that the association between stress and GD was accounted for primarily by escapism from the self rather than by escapism from the world. Hypothesis 4
The effect of EW and ES on well-being and vitality.

To examine not only the negative but also the potential positive effects of escapism, we tested its predictive power for well-being and vitality. A multiple regression analysis was conducted with ES and EW as predictors. The overall model predicting vitality was significant, F(2, 139) = 9.36, p < .001, R
2 = .12, and the overall model predicting well-being was also significant, F(2, 139) = 12.52, p < .001, R
2 = .15.

ES was a significant negative predictor of both outcome variables, whereas EW was not significantly related to either (see Table 4 ). These results suggest that while EW may encompass both adaptive and maladaptive functions depending on individual and situational factors, ES appears to be consistently associated with reduced well-being and vitality.

The present study provides novel insights into the motivational etiology of GD by differentiating between two forms of escapism: escapism from the world (EW) and escapism from the self (ES). Consistent with Hypothesis 1, ES accounted for a significant proportion of the variance in GD beyond that explained by EW. In contrast, when the variance explained by ES was taken into account, EW did not contribute substantially to the prediction of GD. This finding highlights the central role of self-related processes in problematic gaming. Although both forms of escapism were correlated with GD, the hierarchical regression analyses demonstrated that only ES uniquely explained variance in the disorder. This pattern is consistent with Baumeister and Scher's (1988) conceptualization of escapism insofar as it suggests that the maladaptive potential of escape lies primarily in the avoidance of aversive self-awareness rather than in mere withdrawal from external reality.

Supporting Hypothesis 2, mediation analyses demonstrated that the relationship between EW and GD was statistically accounted for by ES. In other words, distancing oneself from the external world contributes to gaming disorder particularly when it is associated with avoidance of the self. This result underscores the importance of distinguishing between external and internal targets of escape, and complements earlier research by Kwon et al. (2009), who identified self-discrepancy and negative mood as key mechanisms linking escapism to problematic outcomes. In this sense, our findings suggest that the maladaptive aspect of escapism lies not in disengagement from the world per se, but in the self-avoidant function that such disengagement may come to serve. In line with Hypothesis 3, ES, but not EW, mediated the relationship between stress and GD. This finding extends the results of Maroney et al. (2018), who emphasized the role of the escape motive in translating stress into problematic gaming. The current results suggest that not every form of escape is equally maladaptive: stress was linked to problematic gaming specifically through escapism from the self, whereas escapism from the world did not account for this association. This pattern is consistent with the view that gaming-related escape becomes particularly problematic when it serves a self-avoidant function rather than merely reflecting disengagement from external stressors. At the same time, this interpretation should remain cautious, as the present measures did not assess the temporal persistence of these tendencies directly, and the results were based on a relatively small sample, which may have limited the stability of the parameter estimates.

Finally, the analysis of positive outcomes (Hypothesis 4) revealed that ES was negatively associated with both well-being and vitality, whereas EW showed no significant relationship. These findings resonate with the model of escapism proposed by Kosa and Uysal (2020, pp. 63–76) and with evidence suggesting that distraction from unmanageable external stressors may in certain contexts facilitate recovery and mood regulation. By contrast, escape rooted in the rejection of one's self-image appears consistently harmful. However, given the relatively small sample size, these findings should be treated as preliminary and in need of replication in larger and more diverse populations.

Taken together, these results highlight the importance of refining the construct of escapism in gaming research. Many prior studies conceptualized escapism primarily as withdrawal from reality (e.g., Yee, 2006; Demetrovics et al., 2011; Giardina et al., 2024). Our findings suggest that this “world-focused” approach overlooks the inner dimension of escape. Distinguishing EW from ES provides a more nuanced understanding of why escapism may at times be beneficial, while at other times strongly associated with GD and diminished well-being.

The distinction between escapism from the world and escapism from the self carries important implications for both prevention and intervention efforts. First, it suggests that interventions should not aim at reducing escapism as such, since temporary withdrawal from external demands may serve adaptive functions such as stress regulation, mood management, and recovery. Instead, the focus should be placed on maladaptive escapism, specifically the entrenched avoidance of the self, which our findings indicate as the central pathway linking escapism to GD.

From a preventive perspective, public health campaigns and educational settings could frame escapism not as inherently negative but as a multifaceted phenomenon, encouraging young people to use games strategically for recovery while remaining mindful of the risks of self-avoidant play.

Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the study was based on a relatively small and homogeneous sample of young, first-year university students, which limits the generalizability of the findings to other age groups, educational backgrounds, and non-student populations. The modest sample size may also have affected the stability of the parameter estimates, particularly in the mediation and moderation models, and therefore replication in larger and more diverse samples is needed. Second, although the present study was based on the first wave of a longitudinal project, the analyses reported here were cross-sectional and do not allow conclusions about causality or temporal precedence. Accordingly, the observed associations may also reflect reverse or bidirectional relationships. Third, the study relied exclusively on self-report measures, which may be influenced by reporting biases such as social desirability and recall bias. Finally, the EW/ES scale is a newly developed measure and, although it showed promising initial properties, it requires further validation in independent and more diverse samples before it can be considered firmly established.

By differentiating escapism from the world and escapism from the self, the present study advances the theoretical understanding of gaming motives and their role in problematic play. Our findings suggest that the maladaptive potential of escapism lies not in withdrawal from external stressors, but in avoidance of the self, which constitutes a key mechanism in the etiology of GD.
